events.description: U.S.-Taliban withdrawal agreement signed (about three weeks before recording). Two Taliban spokesmen said the same day that attacks on the Afghan government would continue.
Esper, days after the Taliban stepped up attacks, suggested Taliban 'hardliners' were failing to honor an agreement to reduce violence.
McKenzie told the Senate Armed Services Committee that a Taliban 'splinter' might be carrying out the attacks ('last week').
Cutoff date of Roggio's tally: 248 Taliban-claimed attacks on Afghan forces in 28 of 34 provinces since the deal, and zero on al-Qaeda.
Taliban statement announced an offensive against ISIS in Kunar province.
Khalilzad tweeted praise for the Taliban offensive against ISIS in Kunar.
Suhail Shaheen replied on Twitter that the Taliban had always fought ISIS and the fight was not part of the U.S. deal.
Al-Qaeda released a three-page Arabic statement praising the Taliban victory, calling Akhundzada 'emir of the faithful', and urging all mujahideen to abide by the deal.
JNIM said it would negotiate with the Malian government if France leaves the region.

key_claims: The U.S. military and officials are 'wishcasting': portraying Taliban attacks as the work of splinters or hardliners, even though the Taliban claim them publicly.

The agreement contains no ceasefire or reduction-in-violence commitment; the Taliban said so the day it was signed and resumed full-scale operations (248 claimed attacks in 28 of 34 provinces as of March 15).

The only specific al-Qaeda provision is that the Taliban will not let al-Qaeda plan attacks against the U.S. or its allies; there is no sign the Taliban have denounced or targeted al-Qaeda, with zero attacks on it.
The Taliban fight ISIS because ISIS rejects the Islamic Emirate, while al-Qaeda is loyal to the Emirate, so the anti-ISIS fight does not mirror any al-Qaeda commitment.
Al-Qaeda sees the deal as an unequivocal win, calls Hibatullah Akhundzada 'emir of the faithful', and urged all mujahideen to abide by it.
Akhtar Mansour, the second Taliban emir, was pro-al-Qaeda, and Akhundzada has not disavowed al-Qaeda or its leader's allegiance to him.
Al-Qaeda affiliates, including JNIM in West Africa and AQIM, are using the deal as a template to demand French withdrawal and negotiate with governments on their own terms.
